title: Thread, Needle and Knot
bigQuestion: How can a needle and a piece of thread hold two pieces of cloth together?

story.title: The Bear With the Open Side
story.kicker: A stuffed bear, a torn seam, and a stitch that held for good.
paragraphs: Maya's bear was named Biscuit. He was brown and soft and older than she was. One morning she found white stuffing on her pillow. Biscuit had a hole in his side, right along the seam. Every time she squeezed him, more stuffing came out.

Her grandmother took a small tin box from a shelf. Inside were needles, a spool of brown thread, pins in a little cushion, and a pair of small scissors. "This is a sewing kit," she said. "Everything you need to fix a seam is in here."

Grandma showed Maya how to wet the end of the thread and push it through the eye of the needle. Then she tied a knot at the end. "The knot is the anchor," she said. "Without it, the thread pulls right through the cloth."

Maya pushed the stuffing back inside. She pinned the two edges of the hole together. Then she made small stitches, in and out, along the seam. Grandma said the stitches should be close together, like footprints in snow.

When she reached the end, Grandma showed her how to tie off the thread with two tiny knots. Maya snipped the tail. She squeezed Biscuit hard. No stuffing came out. The seam held. She had fixed it herself.
story.think: Grandma called the knot the anchor. What would have happened to Maya's first stitch without it?

lessons.title: Seven Tools in a Tin
lessons.mainIdea: A sewing kit holds a few small tools, and each one has one clear job.
reading: Open the tin. Inside is a small pile of tools. A *needle* is a thin steel stick with a point on one end and a hole on the other. The hole is called the eye. Thread goes through the eye. The point goes through the cloth.

A spool of thread is a small tube wrapped in thread. Pins are like needles with no eye and a round head. Pins hold cloth in place before you sew. They live in a *pincushion*, a small stuffed pillow that keeps the points covered.

Small scissors cut thread. A *thimble* is a little metal cap for your middle finger. It pushes the needle without hurting your skin. Learn each tool's name and job. Then put each one back in its place when you are done.

words.d: a thin steel tool with a point on one end and a hole, the eye, on the other
a small stuffed pillow that holds pins and needles safely
a small cap worn on the middle finger to push the needle

look.title: Sort the Kit
look.text: On the table: a spool of blue thread, a needle, six pins with round heads, a pincushion, small scissors, a thimble. Mia wants to hold two pieces of cloth together before she sews. Then she wants to sew them. Then she wants to cut the thread.
look.prompt: Which tool does Mia use for each of the three jobs? Which tool has an eye?

check.q: What is the eye of a needle?
choices: The hole the thread goes through
The round head on a pin
check.why: The eye is the hole at the blunt end. Thread goes through the eye.

check.q: Which tool holds cloth in place before you sew?
check.why: Pins hold two layers of cloth together until the stitches are in.

check.q: Where do needles and pins go when you are not using them?
check.why: The pincushion covers the points so nobody gets poked.

lessons.title: Sharp Rules for Needles and Pins
lessons.mainIdea: Needles and pins are sharp tools, so you count them, cover them and never put them in your mouth.
reading: A pin rolls off a table and lands on the rug. Later someone steps on it. That hurts, and it can be hard to find. Sharp tools need sharp rules. Rule one: count your pins before you start. Count them again when you finish.

Rule two: pins go in the *pincushion*, never in your mouth. Some people hold pins in their lips to keep hands free. Do not do this. A pin can be swallowed. Rule three: pass a needle or pin with the point away from the other person.

Rule four: a needle is small and rolls easily. Keep it stuck in the pincushion or a scrap of cloth when it is not in your hand. If a needle or pin *falls*, stop and find it right away. Tell a grown-up if you cannot find it.

words.d: the stuffed holder where every pin and needle goes when not in use
drops to the floor; a dropped pin must be found before anyone steps on it

look.title: What Went Wrong?
look.text: Jonah starts with 10 pins. He holds three in his lips while he pins a seam. He sets the needle on the edge of the desk. When he is done, he puts 8 pins back in the cushion and goes to lunch.
look.prompt: Find three things Jonah did that break the sharp rules. What should he do before lunch?

check.q: Why do you count your pins before and after sewing?
choices: To see how many colors you have
To make sure none are lost on the floor
check.why: A missing pin can end up in a rug or a chair. Counting tells you if one is lost.

check.q: Where should pins go while you sew?
check.why: Pins go in the pincushion. A pin in your mouth can be swallowed.

check.q: How do you hand a needle to a friend?
check.why: Pass any sharp tool with the point away from the other person.

lessons.title: Choosing the Thread
lessons.mainIdea: Pick thread that matches the color of the cloth and is strong enough for the job.
reading: You have a red shirt with a torn seam and a drawer of thread. Which spool? Hold each spool against the cloth. The one that almost disappears is the right *match*. Stitches in matching thread are hard to see. Stitches in white thread on red cloth stand out.

Thread also has strength. All-purpose thread is the everyday kind. It works for shirts, pillows and felt. Heavy thread is thicker. It is for jeans, canvas and buttons that get pulled a lot. Very thin thread breaks if you pull hard.

Cut a piece of thread about as long as your arm, from fingertip to shoulder. Longer thread tangles. Shorter thread runs out too soon. Cut it with scissors at a slant. A clean, slanted end slides through the eye more easily than a chewed end.

words.d: thread that is the same color as the cloth so stitches are hard to see
the everyday thread that works for most cloth and most repairs

look.title: Which Spool?
look.text: Three jobs. Job A: a torn seam on a navy blue school shirt. Job B: a button on a pair of jeans that gets pulled every day. Job C: a yellow felt bookmark with a yellow stitch design. The drawer has thin white thread, all-purpose navy thread, heavy navy thread, and all-purpose yellow thread.
look.prompt: Match each job to a spool. Why does the jeans button need something different from the shirt?

check.q: How do you pick a thread color for a repair?
choices: Hold spools against the cloth and pick the closest
check.why: Matching thread hides the stitches. Hold the spool against the cloth to compare.

check.q: Which thread is best for a button on jeans?
check.why: Buttons on jeans get pulled hard. Heavy thread is thicker and holds.

check.q: About how long should you cut a piece of thread?
choices: About the length of your arm
check.why: Fingertip to shoulder is long enough to sew but short enough not to tangle.

sections.title: Thread the Needle, Tie the Knot

lessons.title: Through the Eye
lessons.mainIdea: Cut the thread at a slant, hold the needle still, and push the thread through the eye in good light.
reading: Sit near a window or a lamp. Hold the needle in one hand with the eye up. Hold the thread in the other hand, close to the end, about a finger-width back. A long floppy end bends away from the eye. A short stiff end goes straight in.

Push the thread toward the eye. If it misses, do not jab. Snip the end again at a *slant* and try again. Some people wet the end of the thread on their lip to make it stiff. When the tip pokes through, pinch it and pull it out the other side.

Pull until about a hand's length of thread hangs on one side. The long side is the one you sew with. A *needle threader* is a small wire loop that helps. Push the loop through the eye, put the thread in the loop, and pull the loop back out.

words.d: a cut at an angle, which makes a sharp thread end that fits the eye
a small wire loop that pulls thread through the eye for you

look.title: The Thread Keeps Missing
look.text: Leo is trying to thread a needle in the dark corner of the room. He holds the thread by the middle, so a long piece flops around near the eye. The end of the thread is fuzzy because he bit it off. He has tried ten times.
look.prompt: Name three changes Leo could make so the thread goes through on the next try.

check.q: How far from the end of the thread should you hold it?
choices: About a finger-width from the end
check.why: Holding close to the end keeps the tip stiff so it goes straight into the eye.

check.q: The thread end is fuzzy and will not go in. What do you do?
check.why: A fresh cut at a slant makes a sharp end that fits the eye.

check.q: What does a needle threader do?
choices: Pulls the thread through the eye
check.why: The wire loop goes through the eye, catches the thread, and pulls it back through.

lessons.title: The Anchor Knot
lessons.mainIdea: A knot at the end of the thread stops it from pulling through the cloth on the first stitch.
reading: Thread the needle and let one end hang long. Now make the *knot* on the long end. Wrap the thread once around your pointer finger. Roll the loop off your finger with your thumb. Pull the loop down to the end of the thread. It tightens into a small knot.

One knot is small. Some cloth is loose, like felt or knit, and a small knot slips right through the holes. For loose cloth, tie the knot two or three times in the same spot. The knot gets bigger and holds.

Try the first stitch. Push the needle up from the back of the cloth. Pull the thread through until the knot stops it. If the knot pops through, the knot was too small. If it stops with a gentle tug, you have an *anchor*.

words.d: a tight loop tied at the end of the thread so it cannot slip through the cloth
the knot that holds the thread in place at the start of the sewing

look.title: Order the Steps
look.text: The steps for tying a knot are mixed up. Pull the loop down to the end of the thread. Wrap the thread around your pointer finger. Thread the needle. Roll the loop off your finger with your thumb.
look.prompt: Put the four steps in the right order. What is the last thing that should happen?

check.q: Why do you tie a knot at the end of the thread?
choices: So the thread does not pull through the cloth
check.why: The knot anchors the thread. Without it the first stitch pulls straight through.

check.q: Your knot keeps popping through the felt. What should you do?
choices: Tie the knot two or three times in one spot
check.why: A bigger knot cannot fit through the loose holes in felt.

check.q: Where does the first stitch start?
choices: In the middle of the thread
From the back of the cloth
Off the edge of the cloth
check.why: Start from the back so the knot is hidden on the wrong side.

lessons.title: Two Sides of Cloth
lessons.mainIdea: Cloth has a right side and a wrong side, and knots and messy ends belong on the wrong side.
reading: Turn a shirt inside out. The colors look duller. You can see the seams and their loose threads. This is the *wrong side*. Turn it back. The bright, smooth side that shows when you wear it is the *right side*.

When you sew, the knot goes on the wrong side. Loose thread ends go on the wrong side. Then the right side looks clean. If a stitch line has the knot on the front, it shows, and it can catch on things.

Before you sew two pieces together, put the right sides facing each other. Pin them. Sew along the edge. When you turn them right side out, the *seam* is hidden inside. This one habit is the secret to neat sewing.

words.d: the side of the cloth meant to show, the brighter side
the inside or back of the cloth, where knots and seams hide
the line of stitches that joins two pieces of cloth

look.title: Inside or Outside?
look.text: Ava sewed two squares of printed cloth together to make a little pillow. She put the printed sides facing out while she sewed. Now the seam and the knot are on the outside of the pillow, and the loose ends show.
look.prompt: What should Ava have done with the two squares before she sewed? How would the pillow look then?

check.q: Which side of the cloth shows when you wear it?
check.why: The right side is the bright, smooth side meant to be seen.

check.q: Where should the knot end up?
check.why: Knots and loose ends hide on the wrong side so the front looks clean.

check.q: How do you place two pieces before sewing them together?
choices: One on top of a pin
check.why: Right sides together means the seam is hidden inside when you turn it out.

lessons.title: The Running Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The running stitch goes in and out in a straight line and is the fastest stitch to learn.
reading: Pin two scraps of cloth together. Push the needle up from the back at your starting point. Pull until the knot stops it. Now push the needle down through the cloth a little way ahead. Then up again. Down again. In and out, like a dolphin jumping.

Keep the stitches small and even. About the width of a grain of rice is a good size. Keep the space between stitches the same as the stitch. A *running stitch* that is too long and loose will let the seam gap open.

Pull the thread gently after each few stitches. Do not yank. If you pull too hard, the cloth bunches up like a crumpled paper. If you pull too little, the thread hangs in loops. Just snug is the goal.

words.d: a line of small in-and-out stitches, the basic stitch for joining cloth
pulled just tight enough, not loose and not so tight the cloth bunches

look.title: Three Practice Lines
look.text: On a practice square, three lines of running stitch. Line 1: stitches the size of a grain of rice, even spaces, cloth flat. Line 2: stitches as long as a fingernail, big gaps between them. Line 3: tiny stitches, but the cloth is bunched up like a wrinkle.
look.prompt: Which line is done right? What went wrong on the other two, and what would you change?

check.q: How does the running stitch move through the cloth?
choices: In and out in a line
check.why: The running stitch goes up and down through the cloth in a straight line.

check.q: About how long should each running stitch be?
check.why: Small, even stitches about the size of a grain of rice hold well.

check.q: The cloth bunched up as you sewed. What happened?
choices: You pulled the thread too tight
check.why: Pulling too hard gathers the cloth. Pull just snug.

lessons.title: The Back Stitch
lessons.mainIdea: The back stitch goes one step back and two steps forward, which makes a seam that will not pull open.
reading: A running stitch is fast, but you can slide it open with your fingers. A seam on a bear or a shirt gets pulled every day. It needs the *back stitch*. The back stitch makes a solid line with no gaps, like the stitches on store-bought clothes.

Start with the knot on the back. Bring the needle up. Make one running stitch forward. Now go backward: push the needle down at the end of the stitch you just made. Bring it up one stitch length ahead of the thread. Go back down into the end of the last stitch again.

Each stitch fills the gap the last one left. From the front, the line looks like a solid dashed pencil line with no spaces. The seam is *strong* because every stitch is locked into the one before it. Use it anywhere the cloth gets pulled.

words.d: a stitch that goes back into the last stitch each time, making a solid strong line
able to hold when pulled; the back stitch is stronger than the running stitch

look.title: Which Stitch for the Job?
look.text: Four jobs. A: a torn seam on the seat of a pair of pants. B: a quick line to hold two pieces in place while you check the fit. C: the side seam of a stuffed animal that gets hugged. D: a decorative line of stitches on a felt bookmark that is never pulled.
look.prompt: Which jobs need the back stitch? Which could use the running stitch? Explain each choice.

check.q: Why is the back stitch stronger than the running stitch?
choices: Each stitch locks into the one before it
check.why: Going back into the last stitch fills the gaps and locks the line.

check.q: What does a back stitch line look like from the front?
choices: A solid line with no gaps
check.why: Because each stitch fills the last gap, the line is solid.

check.q: Which seam most needs the back stitch?
choices: A quick line to check the fit
A line you plan to pull out
The seam on the seat of pants
check.why: Seams that get pulled every day need the strongest stitch.

lessons.title: Tie It Off
lessons.mainIdea: End every line of sewing with a small knot on the wrong side, then snip the tail.
reading: You reach the end of the seam. If you just cut the thread, the stitches will slide out one by one. You need a *finishing knot*. Push the needle to the wrong side. Take one tiny stitch, right on top of the last stitch, but do not pull it tight.
A small loop is left. Pass the needle through the loop. Now pull it snug. That is one knot. Do it again in the same spot. Two knots hold better than one. Some sewers do it three times on loose cloth.

Snip the thread about a fingernail's length past the knot. Do not cut right at the knot, or it can come undone. Then check the right side. It should be clean, with no knots showing. Put the needle back in the pincushion and count your pins.

words.d: the small knot tied at the end of a seam so the stitches cannot slide out
the short end of thread left after the knot, snipped a little past the knot

look.title: Why Did the Seam Come Undone?
look.text: Sam sewed a neat back stitch along a pouch. At the end he cut the thread right at the cloth, with no knot. He counted his pins and put everything away. A week later the last few stitches had slipped out and the pouch was opening at one end.
look.prompt: What step did Sam skip? Write the three steps he should have done at the end.

check.q: What happens if you cut the thread with no finishing knot?
check.why: With no knot, nothing holds the last stitch, and the line slowly comes undone.

check.q: How is the finishing knot made?
choices: Tiny stitch, pass the needle through the loop, pull snug
Tie the two ends of the thread together
Push a pin through the knot
check.why: A tiny stitch leaves a loop; the needle goes through it and you pull it snug.

check.q: How far past the knot do you snip the tail?
check.why: A short tail keeps the knot from pulling apart. Cutting at the knot can undo it.

review.why: A needle has a point and an eye. A pin has a point and a round head.

review.q: Where do pins go while you sew?
review.why: Pins go in the pincushion so no one is poked and none are swallowed.

review.q: Why do you tie a knot before the first stitch?
choices: So the thread does not pull through the cloth
review.why: The knot is the anchor. Without it, the first stitch pulls straight through.

review.q: Which side of the cloth do knots belong on?
review.why: Knots and loose ends hide on the wrong side so the front is clean.

review.q: Which stitch makes a solid line that will not pull open?
review.why: The back stitch locks each stitch into the last one.

review.q: How long should you cut a piece of thread?
choices: About the length of your arm
review.why: Fingertip to shoulder is long enough to sew and short enough not to tangle.

review.q: The cloth bunched up while you sewed. What went wrong?
choices: You pulled the thread too tight
The knot was on the wrong side
The pins were too far apart
review.why: Pulling too hard gathers the cloth. Pull just snug.

review.q: What is the last step of a line of sewing?
choices: Cut the thread at the cloth
Tie a finishing knot on the wrong side and snip the tail
review.why: A finishing knot holds the stitches. Then snip a short tail.
